summary: order-service's p99 (~5.2s) and its statement timeouts on "INSERT INTO orders" are the downstream symptom of ledger-db contention caused by an un-indexed query shipped in portfolio-service v4.5.0 (dep-5905, deployed 08:56:00Z). That deploy, which added a query on trades filtered by account_id + executed_at with no migration, coincides with the degradation onset (08:52-08:56Z bucket), while ledger-db's only slow-query signature is "Seq Scan on trades (rows=48211907)" attributed to application_name=portfolio-service — a signature autovacuum does not produce. ledger-db is a shared DB used directly by order-service, portfolio-service, payment-service and settlement-service, so one caller's full-table scans starve the INSERT path of the others; order-service errors only start at 09:00:42Z, ~4 minutes after the DB-level spike. The DBA autovacuum change (cfg-2903, 08:00:00Z) is rejected on timing: a ~52-minute quiet gap between the change and any measurable DB effect, with client latency inflecting exactly at the deploy. Confidence is medium (0.60) because the causal index assertion and the absence of a host-level ledger-db fault rest on unretrieved schema/index inventory and unqueried DB resource metrics.

ranked_hypotheses.title: New un-indexed trades query in portfolio-service v4.5.0 drives Seq Scans on ledger-db, saturating the shared DB and timing out other callers
ranked_hypotheses.statement: dep-5905 (portfolio-service v4.5.0, deployed 08:56:00Z) added a query on trades filtered by account_id + executed_at with no index/migration. On the 48M-row trades table this becomes a full Seq Scan, producing ~70-148 slow_queries/min on ledger-db and roughly doubling active connections (~60 -> ~127-204). The shared ledger-db (used directly by order-service, portfolio-service, payment-service and settlement-service) becomes IO/connection contended, so order-service's plain INSERT INTO orders waits behind the scan traffic and is cancelled by statement timeout at 09:00:42Z (284 errors to 10:58Z), surfacing as p99 ~5.2s. Origin is the deployment, not order-service and not autovacuum.

causal_chain.claim: dep-5905 deploys portfolio-service v4.5.0 with a new query on trades (account_id + executed_at) and no migration/index
The un-indexed predicate forces Seq Scan on trades (rows=48,211,907) in ledger-db, logged as slow queries with application_name=portfolio-service
ledger-db slow_queries_per_min jumps ~0.77-1.61 -> ~70-148/min and connections_active ~60 -> ~127-204 in the 08:56Z bucket, concurrently with the deploy
Seq-scan IO + connection pressure on the shared DB delays unrelated writes from co-tenants; order-service's db_pool_in_use pins at ~44-48 while INSERTs block
order-service INSERT INTO orders exceeds statement timeout -> canceling statement due to statement timeout, first 09:00:42Z, 284 occurrences to 10:58Z; p99 steps to ~5.2s
portfolio-service, the deployer itself, shows the earliest and largest degradation (~3574ms then ~7.0s from the same 08:56Z bucket), consistent with the offending caller being worst hit
All services reaching the shared ledger-db (order-service, portfolio-service, payment-service, settlement-service) are exposed, explaining cross-service symptoms with no order-service release

assumptions: portfolio-service's new query truly lacks a supporting index on ledger-db trades (deploy description says 'no migration included'; no schema/index inventory was retrieved)
The Seq Scans at 08:58:38Z originate from that new query and not from a pre-existing reporting/job path (application_name only, no query text captured)
ledger-db contention (IO/connections/locks) rather than an unrelated DB-host problem is what blocks the INSERTs; no ledger-db cpu_pct/IOPS metrics were queried

ranked_hypotheses.title: ledger-db host/instance saturation (IOPS throttling, capacity) independent of any application change
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The ledger-db database host itself became the bottleneck — storage IOPS throttling or provisioned capacity saturation — producing slow queries, gauge-high connections and statement timeouts for every direct caller including order-service. Origin is infrastructure/capacity at ledger-db, not application code. Weakened but not fully excluded: the same history pattern (HIST-110 'Slow orders from ledger-db IOPS throttling') exists, and no cpu_pct/disk_used_pct/IOPS metric for ledger-db was ever retrieved, so a pure host-level fault cannot be positively excluded. It remains a live alternative because the observable signature (seq scans -> IO pressure) is also what an under-provisioned host would show.

causal_chain.claim: ledger-db storage/host loses headroom (IOPS throttling or capacity saturation) in the 08:52-08:56Z window
Query latency and concurrent connection count on ledger-db climb (slow_queries ~70-148/min, connections_active ~127-204)
Blocked/queued writes from all ledger-db callers, including order-service's INSERT INTO orders, exceed statement timeout
Every direct ledger-db caller degrades simultaneously (portfolio-service worst at ~7.0s, order-service ~5.2s, both from the 08:56Z bucket)

ranked_hypotheses.title: Concurrent load/lock contention or traffic increase on ledger-db unrelated to the new query (e.g. reporting job, long-running transaction)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: Something other than dep-5905's new query — a reporting/batch job, a long-running transaction holding locks, or a genuine traffic increase — pushed ledger-db past its headroom and produced the statement timeouts. Origin is data/load behaviour on ledger-db. This is the residual 'contention but not the new code' branch; it is retained only at low confidence because the only slow-query signature captured attributes the load to portfolio-service Seq Scans, and there is a same-signature precedent (HIST-111) resolved as an un-indexed report query.
